reader.title: Barnwell County discharges of Black Republicans
bases: The only account says that on July 28 many Black workers were discharged and driven off the farms where they worked, with night riders threatening others, after a Republican meeting (A2).

The discharges rest on one partisan letter by a Republican county officer (A2); a later Washington dispatch reports Barnwell Democratic clubs resolving not to employ Republicans but describes no specific incident or date (A3).

summary.text: The Barnwell County discharges of Black Republicans took place on July 28, 1880, when many Black farm workers in Barnwell County, South Carolina, were discharged and driven from the farms where they worked, the day after a Republican ratification meeting.
The only account is a letter by the county's Republican co-chairman, who described the discharges as part of a campaign of fines, jailings and night-rider threats against Black Republicans.
A Garfield and Arthur ratification meeting was held in the county on July 27, 1880, and Frederick Nix, Jr., wrote that Democrats had tried every way to keep Black people from attending it.

According to Nix, a county order for men to work the public roads for three days beginning July 28 was moved to July 26 once officials learned of the meeting, and only about 25 of four or five hundred men were told of the change.
On the morning of July 28 the men went to their places of appointment to work the roads, but the sub-Commissioners objected to their working.
When they returned home, Nix wrote, many "were discharged and driven from off the farms on which they were working," some of them working for shares of the crop.
Black men who farmed their own land were instead visited by "armed midnight riders" who cursed and threatened them and warned them never to attend another Garfield Republican meeting.

Men who had missed the rescheduled road work were being arrested and fined $10 to $15 or jailed for fifteen to thirty days, and Nix wrote that others were hiding in the woods and swamps to avoid arrest.
Black ministers traveled the county raising money to free church members from jail, and Nix said the men remained determined to vote for Garfield and Arthur.
No report of any arrest or prosecution for the discharges or the night-riding appears in the coverage.

Nix's letter, dated Blackville, August 11, first appeared in the Philadelphia Press and was reprinted on August 26 by The Post of Middleburg, Pennsylvania, under the heading "South Carolina Bull-Dozing."

A Chicago Tribune dispatch from Washington on August 30, headed "Political Proscription," reported that Democratic clubs in Barnwell and neighboring counties had resolved to employ no man who did not support the Democratic nominee, leaving many Black families "homeless" and "practically outlawed," though it named no incident or date.
Both items ran in Northern papers and treated the events as political intimidation; no Black-press or South Carolina coverage of the discharges was found.

accounts.label: Republican county chairman's letter
accounts.gist: After the July 27 ratification meeting, road officials refused Black men's work on the 28th and many were discharged and driven from the farms they worked, while night riders threatened Black landowners.

accounts.label: Washington dispatch
accounts.gist: Democratic clubs in Barnwell and neighboring counties resolved to employ no one who did not support the Democratic nominee, leaving many Black families homeless.

framing.detail: The Post reprinted the Philadelphia Press letter as 'South Carolina Bull-Dozing,' in which the writer called the treatment 'unlawful' and political.
The Chicago Tribune headed its dispatch 'Political Proscription' and called the families 'practically outlawed.'

record_check.dossier: No town given for the discharges; the letter is dated from Blackville
Unnamed employers/landowners (implied by the passive 'discharged'), with sub-Commissioners refusing road work and armed night riders threatening others; attributed to Democrats by the writer

record_check.record: Black workers discharged and driven off farms after returning from road work
record_check.dossier: Supported, but part of a wider campaign in the letter: rescheduled road work used to fine and jail Black men, and night riders threatening Black landowners; one partisan source
One paper carrying the Philadelphia Press letter; a Chicago Tribune dispatch reports the related Democratic-club employment resolutions in Barnwell without this incident

info: July 28, 1880 (the morning after the July 27 Garfield and Arthur ratification meeting), for the refusal of road work and the discharges
Barnwell County; letter dated from Blackville; individual farms not named
Many unnamed Black men ('colored Republicans') who worked on farms, some for shares of the crop; no number given

None of the discharged men were accused of a crime; the writer attributes the treatment to their politics. Separately, men who missed the rescheduled road work were arrested, fined $10-$15 or jailed 15-30 days

Not named; the letter uses the passive ('were discharged and driven'), names sub-Commissioners as refusing the men road work, and blames 'Democrats' generally; armed 'midnight riders' visited Black landowners

sources.note: 'South Carolina Bull-Dozing,' from the Philadelphia Press: letter of Frederick Nix, Jr., Barnwell County Republican co-chairman, Blackville, Aug. 11, 1880; the only account of the discharges.
quotes: on returning home to their families many were discharged and driven from off the farms on which they were working.
Other colored men who are farming on their own land were visited by a band of these armed midnight riders
the unlawful treatment the colored Republicans are now undergoing in this county since the grand Garfield and Arthur ratification meeting

Long piece on South Carolina red-shirt and rifle clubs, chiefly the 1876 campaign; lists 'Blackville' and 'Postmaster Nix' without detail; nothing on the July 28 discharges.
